title: Eton mess
summary: Broken crisp meringue, softly whipped cream and lightly sweetened strawberries, folded together just before serving.
steps: Heat the oven to 110 °C (225 °F) and line a baking sheet with parchment.
Whip the whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks. Add the powdered erythritol a spoonful at a time, whipping until the meringue is stiff and glossy, then beat in the vanilla.
Spread in rough mounds on the sheet and bake 90 minutes. Turn off the oven and leave the meringue inside to dry for an hour.
Meanwhile, toss the strawberries with the erythritol and lemon juice and leave for 20 minutes to draw out their juice. Crush about a quarter of them with a fork.
Whip the cream with the powdered erythritol to soft peaks.
Just before serving, break the meringue into bite-sized pieces and fold it loosely through the cream with the berries and their juice. Spoon into glasses and serve at once.

swaps.note: chill the can overnight and whip only the solid part

dairy_free_notes: Whipped coconut cream is heavier than dairy cream and tastes of coconut, which suits the strawberries; fold more gently, as it deflates if overworked.
tips: Erythritol meringue stays crisp only for a day or two and softens fast in humid weather; store it airtight and assemble at the last minute.

origin.history: Eton mess takes its name from Eton College, where it has long been served at the school's summer events, including the annual cricket match against Harrow. A dish under that name was recorded by the late nineteenth century, though early versions were simply strawberries or bananas with cream; meringue appears to have become standard later.
